title: Iterative divider off ALU critical path
motivation:
The current timed path runs from the forwarding logic through EX and the
combinational ALU, with roughly 150 logic levels. The ALU implements RV32M
DIV/REM using SystemVerilog / and %, forcing Gowin to time a full
single-cycle divider/remainder network even though CoreMark rarely needs
those operations in the measured loop. Removing that arithmetic from the
one-cycle EX path should raise Fmax far more than the occasional multi-cycle
divide can hurt iterations per cycle.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the combinational DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU cases in rtl/alu.sv with a small
iterative divider/remainder unit that is invoked only when the decoded ALU op
is one of the four divide-class RV32M operations. EX holds the pipeline while
the unit is busy, then writes the final quotient or remainder into the normal
EX/MEM register with unchanged RVFI contents. Keep MUL/MULH/MULHU/MULHSU on
the existing combinational/DSP path and preserve the RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS
substitutions. This should turn the common ADD/compare/address critical path
back into a short mux-plus-adder path, reduce divider LUT depth, and improve
median Tang Nano 20K Fmax enough to clear the acceptance threshold.

title: Split RV32M out of the EX critical path
motivation:
The baseline timing report is dominated by the EX forwarding path feeding the
monolithic combinational RV32IM ALU. Because the ALU eagerly builds multiply,
divide, and remainder hardware behind the same result mux used by ordinary
adds, branches, and load/store address generation, every common instruction
pays for the slowest M-extension structures in Fmax. CoreMark contains some
multiplies, but the current 5.4 MHz clock leaves far more fitness on the
table than a modest increase in M-instruction latency should cost.

formal-only branch. The expected win is a large Fmax recovery because the
critical forwarding-to-ALU-to-register path no longer traverses combinational
division and wide multiply logic on normal CoreMark instructions.

title: Tiny BTB branch predictor
motivation: The current core always fetches fall-through and redirects every taken branch or jump from EX, inserting a bubble on the hot loop branches that CoreMark executes repeatedly. A small predictor should improve iterations/cycle without touching the long ALU/forwarding critical path that currently limits Fmax.

title: Shorten redirect hazard loop
motivation:
After DIV/REM were moved out of the combinational ALU, the best timing path
is no longer arithmetic-dominated. The current worst path runs through the
ID/EX register, EX branch/jump redirect generation, IF's flushed-instruction
mux, hazard load-use comparison, and back into the ID/EX register controls.
That path exists mostly because the hazard unit reads source registers from
the already-flushed IF/ID payload instead of from a simpler raw fetch view.

title: Register the IF ID boundary
motivation:
After DIV and REM were moved out of the one-cycle ALU, the best timing path
shifted away from RV32M arithmetic. The current worst path starts in the
regfile/ID area, passes through EX redirect generation, IF flush/NOP muxing,
hazard control, and returns to the ID/EX register controls. That shape is a
consequence of the current unusual fetch/decode boundary: IF/ID is a
combinational bundle, so same-cycle branch, imem-ready, load-use, and decode
decisions all sit in one broad feedback cone. A structural retime that adds a
real IF/ID register should trade a small amount of control-hazard latency for
a much shorter FPGA clock path.

title: Stateless backward branch predictor
motivation:
The previous BTB predictor attempted to recover taken-branch bubbles but paid
for tags, counters, target storage, and a fetch-side table lookup on an FPGA
timing path that is already sensitive. CoreMark still has hot loop backedges
and direct jumps, so there is predictor value available, but it should be
pursued with far less state and no associative/tag machinery.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the BTB idea with a stateless fetch predecode predictor: predict

the current PC and instruction bits, while ID/EX carries that predicted next
PC into EX. EX already computes the resolved next PC; it should flush and
redirect only when the static prediction differs from the resolved path.
This targets the common CoreMark loop-backedge penalty without LUT-RAM,
counters, tags, or a BTB target mux, so the IPC gain should have much lower
Fmax risk than the failed tiny-BTB attempt.

motivation:

IF flush-to-NOP mux from load-use detection, but the same 32-bit mux still
feeds the ID decoder and register-file read addresses on every redirect or
imem stall.

feedback that still exists because IF muxes the ID-facing instruction to a
NOP on redirect even though ID/EX is separately flushed.

title: One-entry loop backedge predictor
motivation:
The previous predictor attempts showed that CoreMark has useful taken-branch
locality, but fetch-side BTB lookup or stateless instruction predecode can
cost more Fmax than the saved bubbles are worth. A predictor for this core
needs to be almost entirely trained from already-resolved EX information and
keep immediate assembly, opcode decode, counters, and tag RAM off the live
imem-to-PC path.

keep immediate assembly, opcode decode, counters, and tag RAM off the live

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a single-entry loop backedge predictor that remembers the last resolved
taken backward conditional branch. IF compares the current PC against the
stored branch PC tag and, on a hit, advances to the stored target instead of
PC+4. The target is learned in EX from the normal branch_target calculation,
so IF does not predecode imem_data or build a target adder. ID/EX carries the
predicted next PC and a predicted-taken bit; EX compares the resolved next PC
with the prediction and redirects only on mismatch, so loop exits and aliases
recover through the existing flush path.

This targets CoreMark's hot loop backedges with much less timing risk than
the failed BTB and BTFNT attempts. It should recover most repeated taken-loop
bubbles while adding only a small registered target, a PC tag compare, and an
EX-side prediction check. Training only backward conditional branches avoids
polluting the entry with calls, returns, and forward error paths.

title: Share RV32M multiply hardware
motivation:
The current champion already removed DIV/REM from the one-cycle ALU path, but
rtl/alu.sv still builds three independent 32x32 products for MUL, MULH,
MULHU, and MULHSU. Prior results show that making all multiply operations
multi-cycle loses useful CoreMark throughput, so the better micro-opt target
is reducing the multiplier cone without changing single-cycle MUL latency.

title: Two-entry fetch skid buffer
motivation:
The current champion has already removed the dominant divider path and the
failed IF/ID and predictor attempts show that adding latency or fetch-side
target logic is too expensive. However, the benchmark still drives about 22%
random instruction-bus stalls, and the existing front end can only fetch the

motivation:

most ordinary RAM stores are not immediately observed by following ALU work.

title: Phase-locked imem stall prefetch
motivation: Prior predictor attempts that selected branch targets, replayed loops, or posted stores lost too much timing or disturbed memory inference. The benchmark still pays many cycles to the deterministic instruction-ready stall stream, and the fixture documents the exact xorshift phase used by both cosim and FPGA timing. A predictor that uses that phase only as a validated hint can target IPC without adding BTB/tag/target logic to the sensitive branch PC-select path.

Add a phase-locked instruction-stall predictor in the fetch stage, mirroring the documented xorshift ready generator to know when the next instruction-side ready bubble is likely. Use the prediction to run a one-entry sequential prefetch/replay buffer: when the fall-through path is linear and the buffer can be filled on a real ready cycle, keep the next PC/data pair available so a later predicted imem bubble can be absorbed without presenting an invalid instruction to ID. The external io_imemReady pin remains authoritative; on any mismatch, redirect, non-linear PC change, or buffer uncertainty, fall back to the current direct-fetch behavior and invalidate the buffer.

The key distinction from earlier branch and replay predictors is that no branch target lookup, immediate adder, or predictor tag compare sits on the IF PC-select path. The predictor state advances from reset in registered form, the buffer output carries pre-decoded raw rs fields so load-use and forwarding keep their short registered-select structure, and redirects simply clear the buffer. If the deterministic stall phase matches, CoreMark should recover a meaningful fraction of instruction-stall bubbles; if it does not, correctness is preserved by the existing handshake and flush rules.
